title: The ages (Avot 5:21)
hook: five for Scripture, ten for Mishnah, thirteen for mitzvot, and on to old age
tomorrow: Saba stands up when an older friend walks in. why bother, at eighty?

segments.voice: Last week closed on a plan: what, when, with whom. A plan to keep learning. Now a new stretch begins, about growing older, and it starts with a birthday.
screen: `A PLAN TO KEEP LEARNING.` → `GROWING OLDER BEGINS.`

segments.voice: The cake is out, the candles are a fire hazard, and the whole family is singing slightly off key. The grandfather at the head of the table, Saba to the kids, blows, laughs, and says the thing people say at birthdays like this: well, what's left for me now? Crossword puzzles? Everyone laughs. It's a joke. Mostly. But there's an old answer to his question, in the Mishnah, and it doesn't say crossword puzzles. It gives every age a job, from five years old to a hundred, and eighty's job might surprise him.
screen: `THE CANDLES ARE A FIRE HAZARD.` → `WHAT'S LEFT FOR ME NOW?` → `EVERY AGE GETS A JOB.`

segments.voice: It's in Pirkei Avot, from a sage named Yehuda ben Tema. At five, he says, Scripture. At ten, Mishnah. At thirteen, the commandments: that's the age of a bar mitzvah. At fifteen, Talmud. At eighteen, the chuppah, the wedding canopy. At thirty, strength. At forty, understanding. At fifty, counsel, the age to give advice. At sixty, old age. At seventy, gray hair. And at eighty: gevurah. Strength, the deep kind, the kind that's left when the easy strength is gone. Listen to the shape of it. Childhood is for taking in. The middle years are for building. And the later years aren't blank pages. Counsel, understanding, a gray head people look to, and at eighty, a strength of its own. The last lines get quiet: ninety, for bending low; a hundred, as if already passed from the world. The Mishnah doesn't pretend. But it never says any age is for nothing. So when the man at eighty asks what's left, the old answer is: something only an eighty-year-old can do. Something to tell a friend tonight: in the Mishnah's list of life's ages, eighty is the age of strength.
screen: `FIVE, SCRIPTURE. THIRTEEN, COMMANDMENTS.` · `FORTY, UNDERSTANDING. FIFTY, COUNSEL.` · `EIGHTY: GEVURAH, STRENGTH.` · `NO AGE IS FOR NOTHING.` · then, large: `EVERY AGE HAS ITS TASK.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing that shows time passing: an old photo, a birthday card, or just the backs of your own hands. Ask what this stage of your life is for, the one you're in right now. Let one task come to mind, and say its name quietly.
screen: `ONE THING THAT SHOWS TIME.` · `WHAT IS THIS STAGE FOR?` · `NAME ONE TASK.`

segments.voice: The ages: Yehuda ben Tema's map of a life in Pirkei Avot, from Scripture at five to strength at eighty and beyond.
Hold onto this: every age has its task, and eighty's is strength. Happy birthday to whoever's turning anything.

notes: Avot 5:21 paraphrased; numbering differs by edition (5:21, 5:22, 5:25). The voice skips twenty (lirdof, to pursue; its meaning is debated) for length. Ninety 'for bending low' (lasuach; some read it as to converse or meditate); a hundred 'as if already passed from the world'. Confirm the renderings.
Trapdoor: commentators (e.g. Bartenura) link eighty for gevurah to Psalm 90:10. Confirm.
